title: Pushes, pulls, friction and magnets
subject: science
strengths: Most of the class can tell a push from a pull, saying a push moves something away and a pull brings it closer.
The class can state the pole rule: opposite poles attract and like poles repel.

modelAnswers.question: A block slides down a rough slope and slows down. Name the force that slows it and explain how it works.
modelAnswers.answer: Friction is the rubbing force between the block and the rough surface; it pushes back against the slide and slows the block down.

modelAnswers.question: The south pole of one magnet is brought near the north pole of another magnet. What happens, and why?
modelAnswers.answer: They attract: the magnets pull together and snap onto each other.

commonErrors.misconception: A magnet attracts every kind of metal.
commonErrors.example: A learner writes on the worksheet that any metal object will stick to a magnet because it is made of metal.

fixIt.prompt: Fix it: name the one metal you can be sure a magnet will pull, then say what you must do with every other metal.
fixIt.corrected: Corrected working: iron is the metal a magnet reliably pulls; every other metal must be tested one by one, because most metals are ignored.

commonErrors.misconception: A magnet attracts every kind of metal.
commonErrors.example: On the exit ticket, a learner expects an aluminium can to stick to a magnet in the way iron is pulled.

fixIt.prompt: Fix it: say why the shine of a metal tells you nothing, and what a magnet does to most things.
fixIt.corrected: Corrected check: magnets ignore most things and only pull a few metals, so each metal is tested instead of trusted by its shine.

nextSteps: Reteach the metal trap, landing that a magnet only pulls iron and a few metals and that each metal must be tested.
Practise reading the N and S pole labels first before predicting attract or repel.
